title: Atoms and nuclear radiation
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank for AQA GCSE Physics (8463) (review status in the bank: authored-gated-unreviewed). Terms: 4.4.2-c15, 4.4.2-c23, 4.4.2-c10, 4.4.2-c01. Clues: 4.4.2-c15 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.4.2-c23 written for the game from the bank's definition; 4.4.2-c10 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.4.2-c01 first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: 4.4.2-q23, 4.4.2-q28, 4.4.2-q24, 4.4.2-q29, 4.4.2-q25, 4.4.2-q30, 4.4.2-q26, 4.4.2-q31, 4.4.2-q32, 4.4.2-q27.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Ionising power
items.clue: How strongly radiation removes electrons from the atoms it passes.

items.label: Half-life
items.clue: The time taken for the count rate from a sample of an isotope to fall to 50% of its starting value.

items.label: Beta particle (β)
items.clue: A high speed electron ejected from the nucleus as a neutron turns into a proton.

items.label: Radioactive decay
items.clue: The process in which an unstable nucleus gives out radiation as it changes to become more stable.

questions.stem: Which statement shows that radioactive decay is a random process?

options.text: Each nucleus in the sample decays exactly one half-life after the last.
The decay of the sample speeds up as the number of nuclei drops.
Decay can be started or stopped by heating up the sample.
It is impossible to say which nucleus will decay next, or when.

questions.explanation: Unpredictability of the individual event is exactly what randomness means here.

questions.stem: A worker finds radioactive dust on their overalls. Which statement describes the situation correctly?

options.text: This is contamination, but it is only a hazard if the dust can be seen.
This is contamination; the hazard is the decay of the dust.
This is irradiation, and the overalls have now become radioactive.
This is contamination, and the dust is a hazard by touch alone.

questions.explanation: Contamination is the unwanted presence of radioactive atoms, and the hazard is their decay.

questions.stem: The half-life of an isotope is 6 hours. What does this tell you about a sample of it?

options.text: In 6 hours the count rate from the sample halves.
In 6 hours every nucleus in the sample will have decayed.
In 12 hours the sample will contain no unstable nuclei.
Six hours is half the total time the sample takes to decay.

questions.explanation: The specification defines half-life by the count rate or activity falling to half its initial level.

questions.stem: Fruit is exposed to gamma radiation from a source in order to kill bacteria on it. What happens to the fruit?

options.text: The fruit becomes radioactive and must be stored before it is sold.
The fruit becomes contaminated with atoms from the gamma source.
The fruit is irradiated, so no precautions are needed by workers.
The fruit has been irradiated; it does not become radioactive itself.

questions.explanation: Irradiation is exposure to radiation, and the irradiated object does not become radioactive.

questions.stem: If the decay of each nucleus is random, why does a sample have a definite half-life?

options.text: Because each nucleus waits its turn, so the decays are evenly spread out.
Because every nucleus is timed to decay after the same fixed period.
Because a sample holds so many nuclei that their average behaviour is predictable.
Because each half-life removes half, so two half-lives use up the whole sample.

questions.explanation: Large numbers make the statistics reliable even though each single event is unpredictable.

questions.stem: Why is an alpha emitter more hazardous inside the body than outside it?

options.text: Inside, its strong ionisation is absorbed by cells; outside, skin stops it.
It is never a hazard inside, because a sheet of paper is able to stop alpha.
Gamma is worse inside the body, because it passes through everything.
Alpha is only a hazard if the source is touched with bare hands.

questions.explanation: Contamination puts the alpha source past the skin, where all of its ionising energy is absorbed.

questions.stem: The count rate from a source falls from 800 counts per second to 100 counts per second in 24 minutes. What is the half-life?

options.text: 24 minutes: only one halving takes place
12 minutes: half of the total time
6 minutes: 800 falls to 100 in four
8 minutes: three halvings take place

questions.explanation: 800 to 400 to 200 to 100 is three halvings in 24 minutes, so each takes 8 minutes.

questions.stem: A technician uses a gamma source to irradiate surgical equipment. Which precaution is appropriate?

options.text: None is needed, because irradiated objects do not become radioactive.
Handle the source with tongs and store it in a lead-lined box.
Stand behind a thin sheet of lead, which absorbs the gamma completely.
Rinse the equipment afterwards to wash the radioactivity off.

questions.explanation: Distance and shielding protect against the hazard the source used for irradiation presents.

questions.stem: Studies of the effects of radiation on humans are published and shared with other scientists. Why does this matter?

options.text: So that members of the public can vote on whether the work is right.
So that the government decides which findings should be believed.
So that other scientists check the findings by peer review.
So that the researchers are paid for all of the work they did.

questions.explanation: The specification requires findings to be shared so they can be checked by peer review.

questions.stem: (HT only) The emission from a source is measured, and measured again after 4 half-lives have passed. What is the net decline, expressed as a ratio?

options.text: 1 : 16, as the emission halves four times over
1 : 4, as there are four half-lives in total here
16 : 1, since the emission is now sixteen times less
1 : 8, from doubling the four half-lives here

questions.explanation: Four halvings divide the emission by 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16, written 1 : 16.
